title: The formula of a copper oxide from heating data

stimulus.title: Heating copper in a crucible
stimulus.text: A student places pure copper powder in a clean, dry crucible of known mass and heats it strongly in air. The copper reacts with oxygen from the air to form a copper oxide. After cooling, the student weighs the crucible and its contents.

table.caption: Data from Trial 1
rows: Crucible + copper oxide after heating and cooling

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of copper used in Trial 1. (Cu 63.55 g/mol)

rubric.point: Correct moles of Cu with setup: 0.02000 mol

parts.sample: Mass of Cu = 22.575 g − 21.304 g = 1.271 g. Moles of Cu = 1.271 g × (1 mol Cu / 63.55 g) = 0.02000 mol Cu.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of oxygen atoms that combined with the copper.

rubric.point: Mass of O from the difference and moles of O: 0.0100 mol

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the empirical formula of the copper oxide formed in Trial 1. Show your reasoning.

rubric.point: Cu₂O, from a 2 : 1 mole ratio of Cu to O (consistent with parts a and b)

parts.sample: Mole ratio Cu : O = 0.02000 : 0.0100 = 2.00 : 1. The empirical formula is Cu₂O.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass percent of copper in the product of Trial 1.

rubric.point: 88.82% with setup (mass of Cu ÷ mass of product × 100)

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Natural copper has two isotopes: copper-63 (62.930 amu, 69.15%) and copper-65 (64.928 amu, 30.85%). (i) Calculate the average atomic mass of copper. (ii) Describe the mass spectrum of a pure copper sample: the number of peaks, where they are, and their relative heights.

rubric.point: (ii) Two peaks, at m/z of about 63 and 65, the peak at 63 about 2.2 times as tall as the peak at 65
accept: two peaks at 63 and 65; the 63 peak is taller (69% vs 31%)

parts.sample: (i) Average atomic mass = (0.6915)(62.930 amu) + (0.3085)(64.928 amu) = 43.516 + 20.030 = 63.55 amu. (ii) The spectrum has two peaks, one for each isotope, at m/z of about 63 and 65. The peak at 63 is about 69.15 / 30.85 = 2.2 times as tall as the peak at 65.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Suppose some of the copper in Trial 1 did not react with oxygen. Would the calculated ratio of moles of O to moles of Cu be too high, too low or unchanged? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: Justification: less oxygen is gained, so the mass increase and moles of O are too small, while moles of Cu (from the mass weighed before heating) are unchanged
accept: less O combines, so moles of O are low but moles of Cu are the same

parts.sample: Too low. The moles of copper come from the mass weighed before heating, so they are unchanged. If some copper did not react, less oxygen was gained, so the mass increase, and with it the calculated moles of O, are too small. A smaller numerator with the same denominator gives a ratio of O to Cu that is too low.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: In Trial 2, the student uses the same mass of copper but heats it longer at a higher temperature. The crucible and product now have a mass of 22.895 g. Determine the empirical formula of the Trial 2 product, and explain how the results of the two trials are consistent with the law of definite proportions.

rubric.point: CuO, from 0.320 g O = 0.0200 mol O and a 1 : 1 ratio
The two trials made two different compounds (Cu₂O and CuO); each compound has its own fixed composition, so different compositions do not contradict the law
accept: different compounds, each with a fixed ratio
the law applies to each compound separately

parts.sample: Mass of O = 22.895 g − 22.575 g = 0.320 g = 0.0200 mol O. Cu : O = 0.02000 : 0.0200 = 1 : 1, so the product is CuO. The two trials made two different compounds. The law of definite proportions says each compound has a fixed composition: every sample of Cu₂O is 88.82% Cu and every sample of CuO is 79.89% Cu. Two different compositions mean two different compounds, not a broken law.
